ex: The helicopter's rotor makes a very loud noise.
The wind turbine has a huge rotor with three blades.
Stay away from the rotor when the engine is running.
The engineer checked the rotor of the electric motor.

shrapnel.note: Most often "shrapnel" means metal pieces from a bomb: "He has shrapnel in his leg."
ex: In World War I, armies fired shrapnel at soldiers in open fields.
A shrapnel shell was full of small lead balls.
The museum shows an old shrapnel shell from 1915.
The shrapnel shell opened in the air above the soldiers.

rand.note: Often "Rand" is a name. As money, the plural is also "rand": "fifty rand."

polo.note: Often "polo" means a polo shirt: "He wore a white polo."
ex: They watched a polo match on Sunday afternoon.
In polo, players ride horses and hit a ball.
He learned to play polo when he lived abroad.
The polo team practiced on the field all morning.

default.note: Most often "default" means a standard setting: "by default", "the default password."

ex: Turn on the sprinkler to water the lawn.
The kids ran through the sprinkler on a hot day.
The fire sprinklers came on in the hall.
Our garden sprinkler runs every morning at six.
Termites damaged the wooden floor in our kitchen.
We called a company to get rid of the termites.
Termites eat wood and can destroy a house.
The inspector found termites in the old garage.

prefect.note: In British schools, a "prefect" is an older student who helps keep order.

ex: Put the old bills in the shredder, please.
The office shredder is full again.
We bought a small paper shredder for home.
The shredder jammed again this morning.

cognac.note: Usually uncountable: a glass of cognac. "A cognac" can mean one glass.

styling.note: Uncountable: some styling, a lot of styling (not "a styling").

WTF.note: Very rude slang; use only in texts with close friends.

nectar.note: Uncountable: some nectar, a lot of nectar (not "a nectar").
ex: Bees collect nectar from flowers to make honey.
Hummingbirds drink nectar from bright red flowers.
These flowers are full of sweet nectar in spring.
She ordered a glass of peach nectar with breakfast.
Many Sikhs wear a turban as part of their faith.
My classmate is a Sikh from northern India.
The Sikh temple serves free meals to everyone.
Sikhs follow the teachings of ten gurus.

stretching.note: Often a form of "stretch": "The road is stretching for miles." Uncountable: do some stretching.

em.note: Most often "em" is short for "them" in speech: "Let's get 'em!"
ex: In English, the letter M is called "em."
Is that an em or an en on the form?
The word "summer" has a double em in the middle.
She wrote a big red em on the board.

Baptist.note: Always capitalized. "John the Baptist" is a name from the Bible.
ex: He grew up as a Baptist in a small town.
The Baptists built a new church in our town.
My grandmother is a Baptist and goes to church every Sunday.
Baptists usually baptize adults, not babies.

latex.note: Uncountable: some latex, a lot of latex (not "a latex").
ex: Some people are allergic to latex gloves.
The nurse put on a pair of latex gloves.
Natural latex comes from the sap of rubber trees.
This mattress is made of soft natural latex.

unison.note: Almost always in the phrase "in unison": "They sang in unison."
ex: The choir sang the first line in unison.
The students answered the teacher in unison.
The two guitars played the melody in unison.
The whole crowd shouted the team's name in unison.

pedestal.note: "Put someone on a pedestal" means to admire them too much.

mascara.note: Uncountable: some mascara, a lot of mascara (not "a mascara").

hectare.note: In the US, "acre" is far more common than "hectare".

lira.note: Plural: "lira" for Turkish money; for old Italian money, "lire."
ex: This coffee costs fifty lira in Istanbul.
I changed euros into Turkish lira at the bank.
The lira lost a lot of value this year.
How many lira does a bus ticket cost?

incest.note: Uncountable: some incest, a lot of incest (not "a incest").

zoning.note: Uncountable: some zoning, a lot of zoning (not "a zoning").

citrus.note: Often used before a noun: "citrus fruit".
ex: Lemons, limes, and oranges are all citrus fruits.
I love the fresh smell of citrus in the morning.
Citrus trees grow well in warm, sunny places.
Add a little citrus juice to the salad.

imbecile.note: A rude insult; avoid using it about people.

alcoholism.note: Uncountable: some alcoholism, a lot of alcoholism (not "a alcoholism").

prompt.note: Most often "prompt" means quick or "to cause": "a prompt reply", "What prompted this?"

heroism.note: Uncountable: some heroism, a lot of heroism (not "a heroism").

tract.note: Usually with a word before it: "digestive tract".
ex: The digestive tract is about nine meters long.
She had an infection in her urinary tract.
Food moves slowly through the digestive tract.
The doctor checked his upper respiratory tract.
